subChunks.title: Cloud Cost Management, FinOps & Unit Economics for Engineers
subChunks.hookHtml: Cloud infrastructure bills at the end of the month are not the CFO's problem to understand — they are the Lead Engineer's problem to explain, predict, and manage. The engineers who design and deploy the systems are the ones who determine what those bills will be. Cost engineering is the discipline of making cost a first-class concern alongside performance, reliability, and security.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Why Engineers Must Own Costs

Infrastructure costs are directly controlled by engineering decisions. The choice of database (managed vs self-hosted), the choice of message queue (SQS vs Kafka), the container size and concurrency settings, the caching strategy, the data transfer architecture — each is a cost decision made by engineers, often without a cost frame. A Lead who doesn't track costs will eventually face an uncomfortable conversation with finance about a bill that keeps growing without clear justification.

Key Cloud Cost Concepts

Compute: paid for CPU and memory (Cloud Run: per-request with minimum instances, GKE/EC2: always-on per-instance). Scale-to-zero eliminates idle cost but introduces cold-start latency.

Storage: database storage (typically cheap), blob storage (cheap per GB), and — crucially — egress (data leaving the cloud region is expensive, often $0.08–0.12/GB). Moving large datasets between regions or to end users via unoptimised paths is a common surprise cost.

Managed services premium: Neon Postgres, Confluent Kafka, Datadog — each trades operational burden for a cost premium. The question is not 'is the managed service expensive?' but 'is the managed service premium cheaper than the engineering time to operate the alternative?'

Reserved capacity vs on-demand: on-demand pricing is convenient but expensive for predictable workloads. Reserved instances (committing to 1–3 years) reduce cost by 40–70% for always-on services. Spot/preemptible instances reduce cost by 60–90% for fault-tolerant batch workloads.

Unit Economics: Cost Per User / Cost Per Event

Raw cloud bills tell you how much you're spending. Unit economics tell you how efficiently you're spending. Cost per active user, cost per spell cast, cost per tournament processed — these metrics connect infrastructure cost to business value and tell you whether your infrastructure is scaling efficiently or inefficiently with growth.

If your cost-per-user is flat as you grow (linear cost scaling), your architecture scales inefficiently — every new user adds the same marginal cost. If cost-per-user decreases as you scale (sublinear), you're leveraging fixed costs effectively. If it increases (superlinear), something is scaling faster than users — a problem.

FinOps Practices for Engineering Teams

Cost tagging: tag all resources by service, team, and environment. Without tags, it is impossible to attribute costs and impossible to notice when one service's costs spike.

Budget alerts: set alerts at 80% and 100% of monthly budget per service — not for the total account. Service-level alerts allow early detection of anomalies before they accumulate at month-end.

Cost review cadence: monthly cost review in engineering sync, quarterly trend analysis, annual commitment review (are reserved instance commitments still appropriate for current usage patterns?).

Rightsizing: regularly compare actual CPU/memory usage against provisioned size. An instance consistently at 15% CPU utilisation is over-provisioned and should be downsized. Cloud consoles provide utilisation reports; few teams act on them.

Common Cost Anti-Patterns

Data transfer naivety: logging every event to a cross-region analytics pipeline, streaming raw logs to a monitoring service, or fetching full objects when only metadata is needed — all generate unexpected egress costs.

Dev environments at production size: staging and development environments running at full production capacity 24/7, often with no traffic. Shut down development environments after hours; right-size staging.

Unused resources: databases provisioned for a project that ended, load balancers with no backends, old container images never cleaned up. A monthly 'orphaned resources' sweep pays for itself in minutes.

storyBeats.text: The Academy's cloud bill grew from £800/month to £3,400/month in one quarter. Nobody had noticed. The billing alert was set on the total account, not by service. The investigation revealed three causes: a staging environment running at production scale 24/7 (£600/month for zero traffic), an untagged logging pipeline sending structured logs to a US analytics service from a UK deployment (£800/month egress), and a Kafka topic retaining 14 days of data at maximum retention for a service that replayed nothing (£400/month storage). None of these required technical work to fix — they required someone to look at the bill with a cost frame and trace each line back to a design decision.

storyBeats.speaker: Head of Infrastructure Mira
storyBeats.text: The engineers who built those systems were not careless — they were not thinking about cost. They were thinking about correctness, reliability, and performance. Cost is a non-functional requirement that has to be explicitly included in the design conversation, not discovered at the end of the month. I now ask every architect before they finalise a design: what happens to the cost if traffic doubles? If a feature team enables this integration for all 50,000 users? That question surfaces the expensive architectural decisions before they are locked in.

storyBeats.speaker: Head of Infrastructure Mira
storyBeats.text: Unit economics changed how we talk about cost internally. 'Our monthly bill is £3,400' means nothing to a product manager or a CEO. 'Our cost per active user is 14p/month, and as we scale from 10,000 to 100,000 users we expect it to drop to 9p/month due to fixed cost amortisation' — that is a business case. It also exposes when cost is growing faster than users, which is the signal that something is architecturally wrong.

storyBeats.speaker: Head of Infrastructure Mira
storyBeats.text: The managed service premium question is the one that most teams get wrong. They see Neon Postgres at £200/month and think 'I could run self-hosted Postgres for £40/month.' What they don't count: the SRE time to manage upgrades, backup verification, failover testing, and on-call response. If that SRE time is 3 hours/month and an engineer costs £80/hour, self-hosted is more expensive before you add the on-call risk. Run the full comparison — compute, storage, and operations cost — before concluding the managed service is overpriced.

learningObjectives: Explain the main cloud cost categories (compute, storage, egress, managed services) and identify where each appears in an architecture
Calculate unit economics (cost per user, cost per event) and explain what sublinear vs superlinear cost scaling means
Identify common cost anti-patterns in cloud architectures and propose specific remediations
Describe the FinOps practices (tagging, budget alerts, rightsizing, cost cadence) that keep costs visible and manageable
commonMistakes: Setting budget alerts at the account level only — misses per-service spikes until they accumulate
Ignoring data egress costs — cross-region data transfer is often the largest surprise cost
Treating managed service cost as purely infrastructure cost — missing the operational saving in the comparison
Running development and staging environments at production size 24/7 — significant cost for zero business value
assessmentCriteria: Can break down a cloud architecture into its main cost components and estimate relative cost contribution of each
Can calculate cost-per-user for a given monthly bill and user count, and describe what the trend should look like at 10× scale
Can identify three cost anti-patterns in a described architecture and propose specific, quantified remediations
Can compare managed vs self-hosted options by including both infrastructure and operational cost in the comparison
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to an engineer who thinks 'cloud costs are a finance problem' why engineers are actually the ones who determine infrastructure costs. What is a unit economic metric and why is it more useful than a raw bill number? Give a concrete example of an architectural decision that had a significant but non-obvious cost implication.
subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
The Academy has the following monthly cloud costs:

  • Cloud Run (spell and user services): £180/month
  • Neon Postgres: £220/month
  • Google Cloud Storage (spell assets): £40/month
  • Datadog (monitoring): £350/month
  • Staging environment (Cloud Run + database, identical to production): £310/month
  • Data transfer (structured logs sent to US Datadog endpoint from UK services): £190/month
  • Kafka (Confluent Cloud, all topics at 14-day retention): £280/month

Total: £1,570/month. The Academy has 8,000 monthly active users.

Answer: (1) What is the current cost per monthly active user? (2) Identify three cost reduction opportunities with estimated monthly savings and what trade-off (if any) each involves. (3) What FinOps practices are obviously missing? (4) If the Academy scales to 80,000 monthly active users with no architectural changes, what happens to cost per user?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Current cost per MAU:
   £1,570 / 8,000 = £0.196 per monthly active user (~19.6p/user/month)

2. Three cost reduction opportunities:

   (a) Right-size staging environment — £310/month for zero-traffic environment:
   Action: reduce Cloud Run minimum instances to 0 in staging (scale-to-zero when not in use), downsize the staging database to a development tier (~£30/month vs £220 for a production replica). Estimated saving: £220–250/month.
   Trade-off: cold starts in staging when testing; staging database may not fully represent production behaviour for query performance testing. Acceptable — staging is for functional testing, not production-scale load.

   (b) Egress optimisation — £190/month sending UK logs to US Datadog endpoint:
   Action: switch Datadog intake endpoint to EU region (api.datadoghq.eu). Estimated saving: £150–180/month (egress charges eliminated or reduced to intra-region rates).
   Trade-off: data residency changes from US to EU — for a UK company this may actually be preferred (GDPR compliance benefit). No functional trade-off.

   (c) Kafka retention reduction — £280/month with 14-day retention across all topics:
   Action: audit which topics actually need 14-day retention for replay. Most operational topics (spell events, notification triggers) have no replay consumer — reduce to 24–48 hour retention. Reserve 7–14 day retention for audit/event-sourcing topics only. Estimated saving: £100–150/month.
   Trade-off: reduced ability to replay events for debugging after 48 hours on high-volume topics. Acceptable if event sourcing is not used operationally.

   Total estimated monthly saving: ~£470–580/month (30–37% reduction)

3. Missing FinOps practices:
   - No cost tagging — the bill cannot be attributed to services or teams
   - No per-service budget alerts — only discovering cost spikes when reviewing the total monthly bill
   - No rightsizing review — Cloud Run minimum instances and database tier have never been reviewed against actual utilisation
   - No unit economics tracking — the £0.196/MAU figure has never been calculated or tracked over time

4. 80,000 MAU cost projection (no architectural changes):
   Most of the £1,570 is partially fixed cost (Datadog, Kafka, Postgres, staging). Compute (Cloud Run at £180/month) scales with requests.
   Estimate: Cloud Run at 10× traffic → ~£900/month. Postgres at 10× data → £350/month. Datadog at 10× log volume → £700/month. Other costs roughly stable.
   Rough total: ~£2,900/month for 80,000 MAU = £0.036/MAU.
   Cost per user drops from 19.6p to 3.6p — highly sublinear, which means the architecture scales efficiently. The fixed costs (Kafka, monitoring platform, staging) amortise well across a larger user base.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
You are the Lead Engineer responsible for the Academy platform. You are presenting a cost review to the VP of Engineering and the CFO. The current monthly infrastructure bill is £4,200 for 25,000 monthly active users. The CFO asks: 'Is this reasonable? What will this cost at 250,000 users?'

Answer: (1) Calculate current unit economics. (2) Design a framework for determining whether this cost is 'reasonable' (what would you compare it to?). (3) Project cost at 250,000 users — identify which costs scale linearly, which are fixed, and which might need architectural changes. (4) Recommend three specific investments (each taking 1–2 engineer-weeks) that would reduce cost at scale. (5) Frame your answer for the CFO — a 3-bullet non-technical summary.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
1. Current unit economics:
   £4,200 / 25,000 MAU = £0.168/MAU/month (~16.8p/user/month)
   Annual cost per user: ~£2.02/user/year

2. Is this reasonable? Framework:
   Comparisons:
   (a) Revenue per user: if ARPU is £10/month, infrastructure at 16.8p is 1.7% of revenue — typical SaaS target is 5–15% of revenue for COGS including infrastructure. This looks efficient.
   (b) Benchmarks: B2C SaaS infrastructure costs typically run £0.10–£0.50/MAU/month depending on compute intensity. At 16.8p, we are in the lower half of the range — reasonable.
   (c) Trend: is cost-per-user flat, growing, or declining as we've grown from 5,000 to 25,000 MAU? If it has been declining, architecture is scaling well. If growing, something is scaling superlinearly.

3. Cost at 250,000 users (10× current):

   Linear scaling costs (grow ~10×):
   - Compute (Cloud Run): currently ~£800/month → ~£5,000/month at 10×
   - Database compute (read queries): currently ~£600/month → ~£3,000/month (partly offset by caching)

   Semi-linear costs (grow 3–5×):
   - Storage (database data, assets): currently ~£400/month → ~£1,200/month
   - Egress (data to users): currently ~£300/month → ~£900/month

   Fixed/sublinear costs (stay roughly stable or grow slowly):
   - Monitoring platform: currently ~£700/month → ~£900/month (log volume grows but Datadog pricing has tiers)
   - Kafka: currently ~£500/month → ~£700/month (partition count is the driver, not pure traffic)
   - Staging environment: ~£500/month → stays £500/month (does not scale with users)

   Rough projection at 250,000 MAU: ~£14,000/month
   Unit economics at 250,000: £14,000 / 250,000 = £0.056/MAU — significant improvement (5.6p vs 16.8p today)

   Architectural risk: database read throughput at 10× may require read replicas or caching layer before reaching 250,000 MAU.

4. Three cost-reduction investments (1–2 engineer-weeks each):

   (a) Implement Redis caching for spell catalogue reads (1 week):
   Most read traffic hits the spell catalogue (browsing, search). Caching with 5-minute TTL would reduce database read queries by an estimated 60%. At 250,000 users, this prevents needing a read replica. Estimated saving at scale: £1,500–2,000/month.

   (b) Compress and optimise CDN for spell assets (1 week):
   Spell images and audio files are served from GCS without CDN or compression. Adding a Cloud CDN configuration and WebP conversion for images would reduce egress cost by an estimated 40–50%. Estimated saving at scale: £300–400/month.

   (c) Add database connection pooling at the application layer (PgBouncer or equivalent) (1–2 weeks):
   At 10× users, connection overhead becomes a scaling bottleneck. A connection pooler reduces database connection count (and associated Postgres cost tier) while handling burst traffic more efficiently. Prevents the need to upgrade to a higher Neon plan tier earlier than necessary.

5. CFO summary (3 bullets):
   - 'Today we spend 17p per active user per month on infrastructure — which is in line with industry standards for this type of platform.'
   - 'At 10× our current user base, we project the bill to grow to ~£14,000/month — but cost per user drops to 5.6p due to fixed costs being shared across more users.'
   - 'We've identified three engineering investments (about 4 weeks of engineering time total) that will keep the cost curve healthy and prevent the need for a larger infrastructure upgrade before we reach 250,000 users.'

questions.prompt: What is 'data egress cost' in cloud infrastructure?
options: The cost of storing data in a cloud database
The cost of data leaving the cloud provider's network — either to end users, to another region, or to a third-party service
The cost of processing data in cloud compute instances
The cost of inbound data transfer to a cloud service
questions.answer: The cost of data leaving the cloud provider's network — either to end users, to another region, or to a third-party service
questions.explanation: Cloud providers typically charge for outbound data transfer (egress) but not inbound data (ingress is usually free). Common sources of expensive egress: sending logs from a UK deployment to a US monitoring service, transferring data between cloud regions, serving large assets (images, video) directly from cloud storage without a CDN, and exporting database backups to external storage. Egress costs are often the largest surprise in cloud bills because they are not obviously visible in architecture diagrams and grow proportionally with user traffic and data volume.

questions.prompt: A company's cloud bill is £2,000/month with 10,000 monthly active users. Six months later, the bill is £8,000/month with 20,000 monthly active users. Users doubled; costs quadrupled. What does this indicate?
options: The infrastructure is scaling efficiently — more users means more cost
Cost is scaling superlinearly — something in the architecture is growing faster than users, indicating an inefficiency that will become more expensive as the company grows
This is normal for cloud infrastructure; costs always grow faster than users
The company should move to a different cloud provider
questions.answer: Cost is scaling superlinearly — something in the architecture is growing faster than users, indicating an inefficiency that will become more expensive as the company grows
questions.explanation: If users doubled but cost quadrupled, cost per user doubled (from 20p to 40p). This is superlinear scaling — the architecture is becoming less efficient as it grows, not more. This typically indicates a bottleneck: a component that scales at O(n²) rather than O(n), uncontrolled log volume growth, a data store growing faster than the user base, or a service with no caching that processes redundant work for each user. Identifying and fixing the superlinear component before it compounds is significantly cheaper than addressing it later.

questions.prompt: When comparing a managed cloud service against a self-hosted alternative, it is sufficient to compare only the infrastructure costs (e.g., managed service monthly fee vs VM cost) to determine which is cheaper.
questions.explanation: A complete comparison must include operational cost — the engineering time required to manage, upgrade, back up, and provide on-call support for a self-hosted solution. If a managed database costs £200/month but a self-hosted alternative costs £40/month in compute, the comparison is not £200 vs £40. It is £200 vs (£40 + operational cost). If maintaining the self-hosted database requires 3 hours of SRE time per month at £80/hour, the true cost is £280/month — more expensive than the managed service, before considering on-call risk. Many 'save money by self-hosting' decisions undercount this operational premium.
